```{r}
# load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(ggthemes)
```

# Line Graph

This dataset was produced from US economic time series data available from <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/>. Type `? economics` to learn more.

```{r}
data("economics")

# what is in the data?
```

Create a line plot with the unemployment rate of the US over time:

```{r}

# basic line plot
economics |>
  ggplot(aes(x=date, y=unemploy)) +
  geom_line()
# add theme
economics |>
  ggplot(aes(x=date, y=unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_tufte()

# change color
economics |>
  ggplot(aes(x=date, y=unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color="linen") +
  theme_economist()


```

::: callout-tip
In ggplot2, you use the **`group`** aesthetic in a `geom_line()` plot when you need to explicitly tell R how to group data points together into lines.

**🌶️ Spicy alert**: I am creating a dataset here using some techniques that might be new to you. Don't worry so much about *how* I created the dataset, you should focus on what the dataset looks like.

```{r}
# Example dataset
df <- data.frame(
  time = rep(1:5, 2),
  value = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 2, 5, 8, 11, 14),
  category = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 5)
)

df

```

:::

## Without the needed `group` command

```{r}
# Incorrect: Only one line drawn without group
# with geom_line
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value)) +
  geom_line(color="blue") +
  theme_minimal()

# with geom_path
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value)) +
  geom_path(color="blue") +
  theme_minimal()

```

## With the `group` command

```{r}
# Correct: Separate lines for each category using group

# with geom_line
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value, group=category)) +
  geom_line(color="blue") +
  theme_minimal()

# with geom_path
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value, group=category)) +
  geom_path(color="blue") +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Using `color` (or `linetype`) instead

```{r}
# Automatically groups by color

# with geom_line
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value, color=category)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype=category)) +
  theme_minimal()

df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value, color=category)) +
  geom_line(linetype="dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("hotpink", "red")) +
  theme_minimal()

df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=time, y=value, color=category)) +
  geom_line(linetype="dotted") +
  theme_minimal()

# ??? How to control linetype like color using scale_color_manual?
```



# `possum` data

The possum data frame consists of nine morphometric measurements on each of 104 mountain brushtail possums, trapped at seven Australian sites from Southern Victoria to central Queensland.

There are two different populations (`pop`): `Vic` (Victoria) and `other` (New South Wales or Queensland)

```{r}
#Be sure to install the DAAG package if you've never used it before... 
library(DAAG)
data("possum")
```

# Histograms

::: callout-tip
Histograms are great for looking at the distributions of numeric variables
:::

A histogram for the foot length (`footlgth`) of all possums in this dataset:

```{r}
# simple histogram

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth)) +
  geom_histogram()

# what do you see?

#change bin size

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50)

# not a great choice fo these data
```

You can also customize by color:

```{r}
# use fill in aes for pop
possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, color=Pop)) +
  geom_histogram()

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_histogram()

#what do you see?

# use position="identity" to change how it is plotted

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_histogram(position="identity", alpha=0.5)

```


Some people prefer to use `geom_density` for a smoother effect:

```{r}
# first use geom_density to look at full dataset

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5)

# use geom density to fix data overlap issue
# use alpha
# add theme

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  theme_tufte()
  
# add axis labels

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  labs(x="Foot length (mm)", y= "Count") +
  theme_tufte()
# change colors

possum |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("blue", "green")) +
  labs(x="Foot length (mm)", y= "Count") +
  theme_tufte()


#pass in a filtered dataset

possum |>
  filter(sex=="m") |>
  ggplot(aes(x=footlgth, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("blue", "green")) +
  labs(x="Foot length (mm)", y= "Count") +
  theme_tufte()


```

# Boxplots

::: callout-tip
Boxplots are good for displaying the spread, central tendency, and distribution of one numeric variable.
:::

![Credit: Michael Galarnyk](https://miro.medium.com/max/9000/1*2c21SkzJMf3frPXPAR_gZA.png)

A lone box-plot for one numeric variable (foot length) with some custom colors:

```{r}

# boxplot for footlgth

ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth)) +
  geom_boxplot()


#control color and fill

ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth)) +
  geom_boxplot(color="blue", fill="lightblue")

```

::: {callout-tip}
If only one boxplot, it puts weird numbers on the x axis, you may want to use the theme to hide these numbers.

```{r}

#hide axis elements
# ggplot(possum, aes(y = footlgth)) +
#   geom_boxplot(color = "blue", fill = "lightblue") +
#   theme(
#     axis.text.x = element_blank(),  # Hide text
#     axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), # Hide tick marks
#     axis.title.x = element_blank()  # Hide axis title
#   )

ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),  # Hide text
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), # Hide tick marks
    axis.title.x = element_blank()  # Hide axis title
  )

```
:::

::: callout-tip
Side-by-side boxplots are good for displaying one categorical variable and one numeric variable. One advantage of boxplots over bar plots is that they are able to show a bit about the spread and distribution of the numeric variable!
:::

A side-by-side boxplot to compare the foot lengths between the two populations of possums:

```{r}
# same color for both boxplots use footlgth
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot()

# different color for both boxplots

ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, color=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_tufte()
#alter the colors
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue4", "chartreuse")) +
  theme_tufte()

# add a jitter (this is a personal favorite)
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha=0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue4", "chartreuse")) +
  geom_jitter() +
  theme_tufte()

# clean up

# narrow the jitter using width
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha=0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue4", "chartreuse")) +
  geom_jitter(width=0.25) +
  theme_tufte()


```

# Violin Plot

A violin plot is yet another plot type used to show data distribution. 

```{r}
# violin plot using geom_violin
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_violin() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue4", "chartreuse")) +
  theme_tufte()

# alter colors and theme
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_violin() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue", "blue")) +
  theme_minimal()

# add labels
ggplot(data=possum, aes(y=footlgth, x=Pop, fill=Pop)) +
  geom_violin() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("lightblue", "blue")) +
  labs(x="Population", y="Foot Length (mm)", 
       fill="Population") +
  theme_minimal()
  
```


::: callout-tip
Histograms, Boxplots, and Violin Plots are all different ways to visualize data distribution. Violin plots and Boxplots are especially good for comparing data distribution between groups. 
:::

## In class exersize
Choose one numeric variable from the possum dataset. Create two different distribution plots of that variable (choose from: histogram, density, boxplot, violin). Filter for only one of the populations and then compare across a different grouping variable (other than `Population`). 

- Change the theme
- Change the colors

Then write 3–4 sentences:

- What do you see? (Be specific.)
- What does each plot make clearer?
- What does each plot hide or distort?
